headline: Bay fluke fire as water hits 68 — bucktails and Gulp dominating the drift
subhead: Marine Parkway Bridge producing keeper doormat action on the outgoing tide.
body_markdown:
The bay finally woke up this week, and it's been worth the wait. Water temps climbed to 68 degrees in the back channels — a solid jump from last week's 64 — and that thermal shift has the fluke stacked up like cordwood on the deeper edges.

I've been working the Marine Parkway Bridge area hard, and the fish are responding. Best action comes on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current sweeps bait off the flats and concentrates it in the channel. I'm talking keeper fluke to 6 pounds, with plenty of 18-to-20-inch fish mixed in. The sweet spot is that 25-to-30-foot drop right where the bridge shadow ends — the fish are sitting on that edge waiting for the tide to deliver dinner.

Rig-wise, it's been all about the bucktail-and-teaser combo. Three-quarter-ounce white bucktails tipped with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets in pearl, with a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp grub on a teaser hook 18 inches up the line. Drag it slow on the drift — let the current do the work. The fish want that bait moving just fast enough to flutter, not racing across the bottom like you're trying to catch a cab.

The Cross Bay Bridge has been producing too, especially on the incoming when bait gets pushed up against the pilings. I've been anchoring uptide and casting bucktails into the current seams. Same rig, but bump up to a full ounce to hold bottom in the stronger flow. Had a beautiful 4-pounder there Tuesday morning that absolutely crushed a white Gulp on the drop.

Weakfish are making their presence known too — not the numbers we used to see, but quality fish in the 16-to-20-inch range. They're hitting the same bucktail rigs, but they want it worked a little more aggressively. Lift and drop, lift and drop, keeping contact with bottom but giving that jig some action. Found them staging in the deeper holes behind Canarsie Pier, where the cooler bay water meets the warmer backwater.

Bait situation is solid. Plenty of spearing and juvenile bunker in the shallows, which explains why the bass are starting to show. I've seen some nice 24-to-28-inch stripers mixed in with the fluke, especially around the bridge pilings on the flood tide. They're not in full feeding mode yet, but they're there. Give it another week of warm weather and we should see some real action.

Porgies are thick as thieves on any structure — bridge pilings, old dock remains, even the deeper shell beds. High-low rigs with small hooks and clam or sandworm pieces. Nothing fancy, just good eating fish to fill the cooler while you wait for fluke bites.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon this weekend, which means spring tides and stronger current flow. That should really fire up the bite, especially if this warm weather holds. I'm watching for that first real push of bunker into the bay — when that happens, the bass fishing is going to explode. The signs are all there: bait moving, water warming, and fish positioning on the structure. It's shaping up to be a hell of a summer on Jamaica Bay.
